reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / Gorlin's Syndromes of the Head and Neck
clinicalPearls: A distal arthrogryposis characterised by limited mouth opening (trismus) and pseudocamptodactyly, in which the fingers flex only when the wrist is extended
The finger flexion is 'pseudo' because it is provoked by dorsiflexing the wrist and disappears when the wrist is flexed, reflecting short flexor tendons rather than fixed joint contracture
Trismus limits mouth opening and can impede dental care, feeding and intubation
Foot deformities such as talipes and short muscles may also occur
Caused by autosomal dominant variants in MYH8, encoding perinatal myosin heavy chain
Intellect is normal and the condition is non-progressive
Management is supportive with physiotherapy, stretching and occasional surgical release of tendons or the temporomandibular apparatus
reference.pathophysiology: Trismus-pseudocamptodactyly syndrome is caused by autosomal dominant variants in MYH8, which encodes perinatal myosin heavy chain expressed in developing and neonatal skeletal muscle. Abnormal myosin function alters muscle length and tone during development, leaving the long finger flexors and the muscles of mastication functionally short. The short flexor-digitorum tendons produce the characteristic wrist-dependent finger flexion (pseudocamptodactyly), while shortening around the temporomandibular apparatus limits mouth opening (trismus). Unlike true camptodactyly there is no fixed interphalangeal joint contracture, and the condition remains static after birth.
additionalDifferentials: Other distal arthrogryposis subtypes with true camptodactyly
Isolated congenital trismus or temporomandibular joint ankylosis
additionalInvestigations: Clinical demonstration of wrist-dependent finger flexion and measurement of maximal mouth opening
Molecular genetic testing for MYH8 and a distal arthrogryposis panel
Three-generation pedigree and examination of relatives
Radiographs or imaging of the temporomandibular joint and hands where surgery is considered
Dental and maxillofacial assessment for trismus
Airway/anaesthetic evaluation before procedures given limited mouth opening
redFlags: Anticipated difficult intubation from restricted mouth opening
Impaired dental hygiene and access leading to dental disease
Progressive limitation of hand or jaw function
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is good, with normal intellect and lifespan; symptoms are static and functional limitations from trismus and finger tightness can be improved with stretching, physiotherapy and, in selected cases, surgery.
pitfalls: Mistaking pseudocamptodactyly for a fixed joint contracture and misdirecting treatment
Proceeding to anaesthesia without planning for the restricted mouth opening
Overlooking the autosomal dominant inheritance in counselling
Neglecting dental access problems caused by trismus
